Across the corpus synthesized in this review, a consistent hierarchy emerges. GLP-1 receptor agonist monotherapy — chiefly semaglutide — reliably resolves steatohepatitis and reduces liver fat and transaminases, but its effect on fibrosis is smaller, less consistent, and stage-dependent. An updated meta-analysis of ten trials (n = 1,908) found semaglutide significantly improved MASH resolution without worsening fibrosis (OR 3.48, 95% CI 2.68-4.53) while pooled fibrosis improvement fell short of significance (OR 1.17, 95% CI 0.49-2.80), with histological reversal concentrated in non-cirrhotic disease [@Peng2026Clinical]. A GRADE-assessed systematic review of placebo-controlled trials [@Khan2026Therapeutic] and a twelve-study systematic review spanning semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, and beinaglutide [@Mahoon2026Therapeutic] reach the same conclusion: hepatic fat and biochemical markers respond consistently, fibrosis regression is real but mainly confined to F2-F3 disease, and an umbrella review of 23 meta-analyses found broad benefit across liver, anthropometric, and metabolic domains but rated nearly 80% of the underlying reviews as critically low quality by AMSTAR 2 [@Wu2026Efficacy]. Dual and triple agonism narrows this fibrosis gap. A meta-analysis of six trials (961 participants) of tirzepatide, survodutide, pemvidutide, retatrutide, and cotadutide showed a markedly larger effect on both MASH resolution (RR 3.32) and fibrosis improvement (RR 1.49) than has been reported for GLP-1 monotherapy [@Santos2026Efficacy], and a 34-study network meta-analysis ranked GLP-1/GIP dual agonism highest for MASH resolution (RR 5.21) [@Tang2026Updating]. Tirzepatide's SURPASS-3 MRI substudy and its PNPLA3-stratified post hoc analysis showed liver fat reduction independent of genotype [@Cusi2026Liver], and SYNERGY-NASH achieved MASH resolution in 44-62% of patients versus 10% on placebo [@Amorim2026GLP]. The clinical takeaway is that monotherapy remains adequate — and better studied — for steatosis-predominant, earlier-stage disease, while multi-receptor agonism is the more defensible choice when fibrosis is the treatment target, consistent with the structural framework proposed by Zhou and Dong, in which GLP-1R action is bounded by systemic signaling integrity, baseline metabolic severity, and persistence of exposure [@Zhou2026From].

Read against the broader MASLD and metabolic-disease treatment literature, these findings reflect a decisive shift away from lifestyle intervention as the sole first-line strategy and toward structured pharmacologic management, paralleling an analogous shift underway in obesity medicine more generally [@Henney2026The]. Contemporary reviews of the MASLD therapeutic landscape increasingly frame GLP-1-based agents — alongside resmetirom and emerging multi-agonists — as core components of a stepwise, biomarker-guided treatment algorithm rather than as adjuncts to weight-loss counseling, reflecting growing recognition that diet and exercise alone rarely achieve or sustain the magnitude of weight loss needed for histological regression in most patients with MASH [@Chan2026Pharmacological]. This reframing extends beyond hepatology: gastroenterologists and other non-endocrinology specialists are increasingly positioned as primary prescribers of GLP-1 therapy for metabolic disease, reflecting its expanding role across the obesity-MASLD-cardiometabolic continuum rather than a liver-specific niche [@Alali2026Beyond]. The mono-to-multi-agonist trajectory documented in this review for hepatic endpoints mirrors a parallel evolution across gut-pancreatic peptide therapeutics more broadly, in which increasing receptor multiplicity is being pursued as a general strategy to close the efficacy gap left by lifestyle intervention and single-target pharmacotherapy alike [@Patil2026The]. Because MASLD rarely occurs in isolation from cardiovascular, renal, and broader cardiometabolic disease, the positioning of GLP-1-based therapy set out in this review is best understood as one component of an integrated cardiometabolic treatment strategy rather than a liver-disease-specific intervention [@Tsai2026Metabolic; @QuirinoVela2026The].

Comparative-effectiveness data against SGLT2 inhibitors reinforce this positioning rather than displacing it. In a propensity-matched real-world cohort, subcutaneous GLP-1RAs outperformed SGLT2 inhibitors on HbA1c, BMI, and ALT reduction [@Toffoli2026Comparative], and initiating semaglutide rather than an SGLT2 inhibitor was associated with markedly lower five-year hazards of mortality, hospitalization, major adverse cardiovascular events, and major adverse liver outcomes in a 55,525-patient matched TriNetX cohort [@Khalil2026Efficacy]. A German claims-based cohort similarly found GLP-1RA use associated with lower hazards of major adverse liver outcomes and cirrhosis than SGLT2 inhibitors (HR 0.91 and 0.88, respectively) [@Maier2026GlucagonLike]. Yet combining the two classes is not uniformly superior: three pairwise target trial emulations found GLP-1RA-plus-SGLT2i combination therapy reduced mortality and liver outcomes versus SGLT2i monotherapy, but increased MACE risk relative to GLP-1RA monotherapy alone (corrected HR 1.111) [@Alkuwaiti2026GLP] — a signal that argues against reflexive combination therapy and for outcome-specific sequencing decisions.

Guideline integration is beginning to formalize this evidence, though unevenly across drug classes and disease stages. The first national MASLD guideline identified in this corpus, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, embeds GLP-1RAs within a stepwise, primary-care-anchored care pathway: FIB-4 as first-line risk stratification, elastography for indeterminate or high-risk results, and GLP-1RA consideration in eligible patients with type 2 diabetes or obesity, reserving bariatric surgery and multidisciplinary cirrhosis management for advanced disease [@Zerem2026Clinical]. This stepwise logic depends on accurate at-risk MASH identification, which remains inconsistently defined across the literature. A prospective biopsy-and-MRE study of 413 patients proposed a simplified at-risk MASH definition (fibrosis stage ≥2) and optimized liver-stiffness cutoffs on magnetic resonance elastography (2.8-6.4 kPa) that captured 28% more biopsy-confirmed pharmacotherapy candidates than AASLD-recommended thresholds, improving sensitivity from 50% to 80% for identifying patients eligible for resmetirom or semaglutide [@Li2026Simplified]. Genetic stratification adds a further layer: PNPLA3 I148M genotype did not modify tirzepatide's hepatic fat response [@Cusi2026Liver], but a GLP1R variant (rs761387) was independently associated with a blunted glycemic response to GLP-1RA therapy [@Toffoli2026Comparative], suggesting that receptor-level pharmacogenomics — distinct from lipogenic risk genotype — may eventually inform agent selection even as it is not yet actionable in routine practice.

Several questions remain genuinely unresolved. Durability after discontinuation is the most consequential: because GLP-1R-based hepatic benefit operates substantially through indirect, weight- and inflammation-mediated pathways rather than direct antifibrotic action, benefit is plausibly contingent on continued drug exposure, and none of the trials in this corpus reported long-term outcomes after treatment withdrawal [@Zhou2026From]. Applicability to advanced fibrosis, cirrhosis, and MetALD is similarly unsettled. The phase 2 zalfermin-semaglutide trial in patients with F2-F4c fibrosis, including compensated cirrhosis, found that the zalfermin-semaglutide combination did not significantly improve fibrosis over placebo, though semaglutide alone showed a nominally significant effect (30% vs 16% responders, p = 0.024) — evidence that semaglutide retains some activity in compensated cirrhosis even as combination strategies have not yet cleared this bar [@Loomba2026Efficacy]. More broadly, compensated MASH-related cirrhosis is characterized by a predominance of negative trials across drug classes, reflecting disease complexity and endpoint limitations as much as inadequate drug potency [@Zeng2026Drug], and diabetic cirrhosis management guidance still restricts confident GLP-1RA use to compensated disease [@Kumar2026Management]. MetALD — alcohol-associated injury superimposed on cardiometabolic risk — has no dedicated GLP-1RA trials at all; current practice extrapolates from separate MASLD and alcohol-associated liver disease evidence bases, an acknowledged gap rather than a validated extrapolation [@Pagadala2026Pharmacologic].

Safety in special procedural and inflammatory-disease populations is better characterized but still evolving. GLP-1RA-associated delayed gastric emptying increases retained gastric contents and procedural disruption during endoscopy, yet real-world aspiration pneumonia rates remain low (approximately 0.01-0.05% during colonoscopy, under 0.3% during upper endoscopy), supporting current guidance to continue therapy with structured dietary and procedural precautions rather than routine cessation [@Beig2026GLP]. In inflammatory bowel disease, GLP-1RAs appear safe and are associated with lower hospitalization and surgical risk, though effects on IBD disease activity itself remain unclear pending ongoing randomized trials [@BeniwalPatel2026The]. The long-term hepatocellular carcinoma risk-benefit balance is the least settled question of all: real-world studies and target trial emulations suggest lower HCC incidence with GLP-1RA use, particularly against insulin or sulfonylureas, but this advantage attenuates in comparisons with other metabolically favorable agents such as SGLT2 inhibitors [@Vozza2026GLP], a pattern echoed by the nonsignificant HCC hazard reduction (HR 0.76) in the German cohort [@Maier2026GlucagonLike]; causal inference here is limited by confounding by indication and by the fact that no trial in this corpus was powered for HCC as a primary endpoint.

This review's own evidence base carries limitations that temper these conclusions. The literature is heterogeneous in outcome definition — histological fibrosis stage, MRI-PDFF, FIB-4, and liver stiffness are used interchangeably as "hepatic benefit" across studies — and surrogate and imaging endpoints substantially outnumber hard histologic or cardiovascular outcome trials; an exploratory meta-analysis of real-world cohorts rated its own pooled estimate for advanced liver outcomes as very-low-certainty evidence, appropriately describing it as hypothesis-generating rather than definitive [@Hu2026Glucagonlike]. The review process itself adds further constraints: literature was drawn exclusively from PubMed, without Scopus or Embase coverage, so conference abstracts, preprints, and journals outside MEDLINE indexing are underrepresented; screening and extraction used an automated single-pass pipeline rather than dual independent human review or a formal risk-of-bias instrument; no quantitative meta-analysis was performed, limiting this synthesis to qualitative pattern description; potential publication and reporting bias within the underlying primary and secondary literature — for instance, selective reporting or publication of favorable MASH-resolution or fibrosis-improvement outcomes — was not formally assessed, and no funnel plot or other quantitative test for small-study effects was performed, a limitation inherent to this review's narrative rather than meta-analytic design; and only English-language, abstract-accessible records were retrievable through the search pipeline, introducing a plausible language and publication bias against non-English regional guidelines and trials.

Future research priorities follow directly from these gaps. Head-to-head trials comparing polyagonists against GLP-1RA monotherapy — rather than each against placebo separately — are needed to establish whether the fibrosis advantage seen for dual/triple agonists in indirect comparisons survives direct testing. Biomarker-guided patient selection, combining MRE-based at-risk MASH thresholds [@Li2026Simplified] with emerging pharmacogenomic signals [@Toffoli2026Comparative; @Cusi2026Liver], should be prospectively validated as an enrollment and treatment-selection strategy rather than used only retrospectively. Given that MASLD increasingly sits within a broader cardiovascular-kidney-liver-metabolic syndrome framework [@Tsai2026Metabolic; @QuirinoVela2026The], outcomes research should extend beyond liver-specific endpoints to integrated multi-organ trial designs, and dedicated fibrate and combination-therapy reappraisals suggest complementary, non-incretin pathways still warrant testing alongside GLP-1-based regimens [@Anagnostopoulou2026Therapies].

In sum, the evidence assembled here supports a two-tier clinical approach: GLP-1 receptor agonist monotherapy, principally semaglutide, as an effective and well-characterized option for steatosis-predominant MASLD and earlier-stage MASH, and dual or triple agonism — led by tirzepatide, with polyagonists such as survodutide, pemvidutide, retatrutide, and cotadutide close behind — reserved for patients where fibrosis regression, not just steatohepatitis resolution, is the treatment goal [@Chan2026Pharmacological]. National guideline frameworks are beginning to operationalize this logic through stepwise, biomarker-anchored care pathways, but major uncertainties persist around durability after discontinuation, efficacy in compensated cirrhosis and MetALD, and the long-term hepatocellular carcinoma risk-benefit balance. These gaps, together with this review's PubMed-only, single-pass, non-meta-analytic methodology, mean the present synthesis should be read as an organizing map of a rapidly moving field rather than a definitive clinical practice statement — one that will need systematic updating as head-to-head polyagonist trials, cirrhosis-stage outcome data, and multi-database evidence syntheses mature.
